claims.evidence: Detailed structural models and figures showing these interactions are presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The ribosome varies in size from 2.3 MDa to over 4 MDa across the three domains of life.
claims.source: The ribosome performs the crucial task of translating the genetic code into proteins and varies in size from 2.3 MDa to over 4 MDa across the three domains of life (Melnikov et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Polypeptide synthesis occurs in the peptidyl transferase center (PTC).
claims.source: Polypeptide synthesis occurs in the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), where the ribosome acts primarily as an 'entropic trap' for peptide bond formation (Rodnina, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The ribosome acts primarily as an 'entropic trap' for peptide bond formation.
claims.source: Polypeptide synthesis occurs in the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), where the ribosome acts primarily as an 'entropic trap' for peptide bond formation (Rodnina, 2013).
claims.evidence: This mechanistic interpretation is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The ribosome is naturally the target of a plurality of antibiotics with diverse mechanisms of action.
claims.source: Because of the ribosome's essential role in supporting life, it is naturally the target of a plurality of antibiotics with diverse mechanisms of action (Arenz and Wilson, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome in key functional states remains too low to provide accurate models of non-covalent bonding.
claims.source: Although X-ray crystallography has been central in revealing the molecular basis of many steps in translation, the resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome in key functional states remains too low to provide accurate models of non-covalent bonding, that is, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals contacts, and ionic interactions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the typical resolution limits of X-ray crystallography for ribosome structures.

claims.claim: The development of small-molecule drugs such as antibiotics is hampered at the typical resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome (~3 Å).
claims.source: Furthermore, the development of small-molecule drugs such as antibiotics is hampered at the typical resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome (~3 Å) (Arenz and Wilson, 2016; Yusupova and Yusupov, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature discussing limitations of current structural data for drug development.

claims.claim: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½).
claims.source: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½; Noeske et al., 2015) and Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å (Polikanov et al., 2015), and cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å.
claims.source: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½; Noeske et al., 2015) and Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å (Polikanov et al., 2015), and cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å.
claims.source: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½; Noeske et al., 2015) and Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å (Polikanov et al., 2015), and cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The 'gold-standard' FSC is more precisely a measure of self-consistency of the data.
claims.source: However, the 'gold-standard' FSC (GS-FSC) most commonly reported, wherein random halves of the particles are refined independently and correlation of the two half-maps is calculated as a function of spatial frequency, is more precisely a measure of self-consistency of the data (Henderson et al., 2012; Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Subramaniam et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This interpretation of the GS-FSC metric is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claims.claim: The map-to-model FSC compares the cryo-EM experimental map to the structural model derived from it.
claims.source: A separate measure, the map-to-model FSC, compares the cryo-EM experimental map to the structural model derived from it (DiMaio et al., 2013; Liebschner et al., 2019; Subramaniam et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a definition of a methodological metric, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The structure of the E. coli 70S ribosome was determined to a global resolution of 2.0 Å, with higher resolution up to 1.8 Å in the best-resolved core regions of the 50S subunit.
claims.source: Here we determined the structure of the E. coli 70S ribosome to a global resolution of 2.0 Å, with higher resolution up to 1.8 Å in the best-resolved core regions of the 50S subunit.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the resolution analysis and local resolution maps presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The final maps were generated from two 70S ribosome complexes that were formed separately using P-site tRNAfMet that differed only by being charged with two different non-amino acid monomers.
claims.source: Our final maps were generated from two 70S ribosome complexes that were formed separately using P-site tRNAfMet that differed only by being charged with two different non-amino acid monomers (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design, which is detailed in the Materials and methods section.

claims.claim: Both complexes yielded structures in the same functional state, with similar occupancy of the tRNAs.
claims.source: In both complexes, we used the same mRNA and A-site Val-tRNAVal. Both complexes yielded structures in the same functional state, with similar occupancy of the tRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis of the two datasets.

claims.claim: Neither A-site nor P-site tRNA 3'-CCA-ends were resolved in the individual cryo-EM maps.
claims.source: As neither A-site nor P-site tRNA 3'-CCA-ends were resolved in the individual cryo-EM maps, we merged the two datasets for the final reconstructions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data analysis.

claims.claim: After Ewald sphere correction in RELION, global resolution of the entire complex reached 1.98 Å resolution by GS-FSC.
claims.source: After Ewald sphere correction in RELION (Zivanov et al., 2018), global resolution of the entire complex reached 1.98 Å resolution by GS-FSC, with local resolution reaching 1.8 Å (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the FSC curves and resolution maps presented in the figures and tables.

claims.claim: The local resolution reached 1.8 Å.
claims.source: After Ewald sphere correction in RELION (Zivanov et al., 2018), global resolution of the entire complex reached 1.98 Å resolution by GS-FSC, with local resolution reaching 1.8 Å (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the local resolution maps shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The global resolution reached 2.04 Å using the map-to-model FSC criterion.
claims.source: The global resolution reached 2.04 Å using the map-to-model FSC criterion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the map-to-model FSC curve shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Focused refinement of the 30S subunit improved its map quality substantially, along with its immediate contacts to the 50S subunit and the mRNA and tRNA anticodon stem-loops.
claims.source: In particular, focused refinement of the 30S subunit improved its map quality substantially, along with its immediate contacts to the 50S subunit and the mRNA and tRNA anticodon stem-loops.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the focused refinement analysis, supported by the improved resolution and map quality.

claims.claim: The high resolution indicated by the FSC curves is supported by several visual features observable in the maps, including holes in many aromatic rings and riboses.
claims.source: The high resolution indicated by the FSC curves is supported by several visual features observable in the maps, including holes in many aromatic rings and riboses, as well as ring puckers, the directionality of non-bridging phosphate oxygens in ribosomal RNA, and numerous well-resolved ions, water molecules, and small molecules (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: These features are shown in the figures and are characteristic of high-resolution structures.

claims.claim: The maps reveal known post-transcriptional and post-translational modifications of ribosomal RNA and proteins in detail.
claims.source: The maps also reveal known post-transcriptional and post-translational modifications of ribosomal RNA and proteins in detail (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 6), many of which are as previously described (Fischer et al., 2015; Noeske et al., 2015; Polikanov et al., 2015; Stojković et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The modifications are shown in the figures and are consistent with prior literature.

claims.claim: Elements of the ribosome at the periphery are less ordered, including the uL1 arm, the GTPase activating center, bL12 proteins, and the central portion of the A-site finger in the 50S subunit.
claims.source: As seen in other ribosome structures, elements of the ribosome at the periphery are less ordered, including the uL1 arm, the GTPase activating center, bL12 proteins, and the central portion of the A-site finger in the 50S subunit (23S rRNA helix H38), as well as the periphery of the 30S subunit head domain and spur (16S rRNA helix h6).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM maps, consistent with prior structures.

claims.claim: The resolution of the maps for the elbow and acceptor ends of the P-site and A-site tRNAs is relatively low, likely as a result of poor accommodation of the unnatural substrates used.
claims.source: The resolution of the maps for the elbow and acceptor ends of the P-site and A-site tRNAs is also relatively low, likely as a result of poor accommodation of the unnatural substrates used.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed map quality and the experimental design.

claims.claim: The 30S ribosomal subunit is highly dynamic in carrying out its role in the translation cycle.
claims.source: The 30S ribosomal subunit is highly dynamic in carrying out its role in the translation cycle (Munro et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The 30S subunit exhibits more flexibility than the core of the 50S subunit even in defined conformational states of the ribosome.
claims.source: Previously published structures demonstrate that even in defined conformational states of the ribosome, the 30S subunit exhibits more flexibility than the core of the 50S subunit.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on prior structural studies.

claims.claim: The mass of the 50S subunit dominates alignments in cryo-EM reconstructions of the 70S ribosome.
claims.source: Furthermore, the mass of the 50S subunit dominates alignments in cryo-EM reconstructions of the 70S ribosome.
claims.evidence: This is a known technical consideration in cryo-EM of the ribosome.

claims.claim: Solvation of the 30S subunit has not been extensively modeled in prior structures.
claims.source: Solvation of the 30S subunit has not been extensively modeled, again owing to the fact that it is generally more flexible and less well-resolved than the 50S subunit, even in available high-resolution structures (Noeske et al., 2015; Polikanov et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an observation about prior work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The tight binding of tRNA to the P site is reflected in extensive direct contacts between the tRNA anticodon stem-loop (ASL) and both the 30S subunit head and platform domains.
claims.source: The tight binding of tRNA to the P site (Lill et al., 1986) is reflected in extensive direct contacts between the tRNA anticodon stem-loop (ASL) and both the 30S subunit head and platform domains (Figure 2A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2 and by prior biochemical studies.

claims.claim: The C-terminal residues Lys129 and Arg130 of protein uS9 form ionic and hydrogen bonding interactions with the nucleotides in the U-turn motif of the P-site ASL.
claims.source: The C-terminal residues Lys129 and Arg130 of protein uS9, which are important for translational fidelity (Arora et al., 2013), form ionic and hydrogen bonding interactions with the nucleotides in the U-turn motif of the P-site ASL, and Arg130 stacks with the base of U33 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Arg130 of protein uS9 stacks with the base of U33 in the P-site tRNA.
claims.source: The C-terminal residues Lys129 and Arg130 of protein uS9, which are important for translational fidelity (Arora et al., 2013), form ionic and hydrogen bonding interactions with the nucleotides in the U-turn motif of the P-site ASL, and Arg130 stacks with the base of U33 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The C-terminal tails of ribosomal proteins uS13 and uS19 are not visible in the map, suggesting they do not make specific contacts with the tRNA when the ribosome is in the unrotated state.
claims.source: However, the C-terminal tails of ribosomal proteins uS13 and uS19, which come from the 30S subunit head domain and are lysine-rich, are not visible in the map, suggesting they do not make specific contacts with the tRNA when the ribosome is in the unrotated state.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of density in the cryo-EM map.

claims.claim: Direct interactions between A-site tRNA and the 30S subunit are highly localized to the top of helices h44 and h18 in 16S rRNA and to helix H69 in 23S rRNA.
claims.source: Direct interactions between A-site tRNA and the 30S subunit are highly localized to the top of helices h44 and h18 in 16S rRNA and to helix H69 in 23S rRNA (i.e. 16S rRNA nucleotides G530, A1492, and A1493, and 23S rRNA nucleotide A1913).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model and is consistent with known interactions in the decoding center.

claims.claim: Contacts between the A-site tRNA and 30S subunit head domain are entirely solvent mediated apart from nucleotide C1054.
claims.source: By contrast, contacts between the A-site tRNA and 30S subunit head domain are entirely solvent mediated (Figure 2E) apart from nucleotide C1054, possibly reflecting the weaker binding of tRNA to the A site (Lill et al., 1986) and the need for A-site tRNA conformational dynamics during mRNA decoding (Rodnina et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 2E and by prior biochemical and biophysical studies.

claims.claim: Protein bS21 resides near the path of mRNA on the 30S subunit platform.
claims.source: Protein bS21, which resides near the path of mRNA on the 30S subunit platform (Held et al., 1973; Marzi et al., 2007; Sashital et al., 2014), is essential in E. coli (Bubunenko et al., 2007; Goodall et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Protein bS21 is essential in E. coli.
claims.source: Protein bS21, which resides near the path of mRNA on the 30S subunit platform (Held et al., 1973; Marzi et al., 2007; Sashital et al., 2014), is essential in E. coli (Bubunenko et al., 2007; Goodall et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Structural disorder in the bS21 region has precluded modeling of the C-terminus in prior structures.
claims.source: Although partial structural models of bS21 have been determined (Fischer et al., 2015; Noeske et al., 2015), structural disorder in this region has precluded modeling of the C-terminus.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about prior work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the present maps, low-pass filtering provides clear evidence for the conformation of the entire bS21 protein chain, including 13 amino acids at the C-terminus that extend to the base of the 30S subunit head domain.
claims.source: In the present maps, low-pass filtering provides clear evidence for the conformation of the entire protein chain, including 13 amino acids at the C-terminus that extend to the base of the 30S subunit head domain (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Most of the C-terminal residues of bS21 are found in an alpha-helical conformation near the Shine-Dalgarno helix.
claims.source: Most of the C-terminal residues are found in an alpha-helical conformation near the Shine-Dalgarno helix formed between the 3' end of 16S rRNA and the mRNA ribosome binding site (Shine and Dalgarno, 1975), while the C-terminal arginine-leucine-tyrosine (RLY) motif makes close contacts with 16S rRNA helix h37 and nucleotide A1167 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The C-terminal arginine-leucine-tyrosine (RLY) motif of bS21 makes close contacts with 16S rRNA helix h37 and nucleotide A1167.
claims.source: Most of the C-terminal residues are found in an alpha-helical conformation near the Shine-Dalgarno helix formed between the 3' end of 16S rRNA and the mRNA ribosome binding site (Shine and Dalgarno, 1975), while the C-terminal arginine-leucine-tyrosine (RLY) motif makes close contacts with 16S rRNA helix h37 and nucleotide A1167 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The arginine and leucine residues of the RLY motif pack in the minor groove of helix h37.
claims.source: The arginine and leucine residues pack in the minor groove of helix h37, and the terminal tyrosine stacks on A1167.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The terminal tyrosine of the RLY motif stacks on A1167.
claims.source: The arginine and leucine residues pack in the minor groove of helix h37, and the terminal tyrosine stacks on A1167.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Multiple sequence alignment of bS21 sequences from distinct bacterial phyla revealed that the RLY C-terminal motif is conserved in bS21 sequences of the Gammaproteobacteria phylum.
claims.source: Multiple sequence alignment of bS21 sequences from distinct bacterial phyla revealed that the RLY C-terminal motif is conserved in bS21 sequences of the Gammaproteobacteria phylum while in Betaproteobacteria, the sibling group of Gammaproteobacteria, bS21 sequences possess a lysine-leucine-tyrosine (KLY) C-terminal motif instead (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: In Betaproteobacteria, bS21 sequences possess a lysine-leucine-tyrosine (KLY) C-terminal motif instead of RLY.
claims.source: Multiple sequence alignment of bS21 sequences from distinct bacterial phyla revealed that the RLY C-terminal motif is conserved in bS21 sequences of the Gammaproteobacteria phylum while in Betaproteobacteria, the sibling group of Gammaproteobacteria, bS21 sequences possess a lysine-leucine-tyrosine (KLY) C-terminal motif instead (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: C-terminal extensions (RLY or KLY) are absent in bS21 from other bacterial phyla.
claims.source: Interestingly, such C-terminal extensions (RLY or KLY) are absent in other bacterial phyla (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Putative homologs of bS21 were identified in huge bacteriophages.
claims.source: Recently, putative homologs of bS21 were identified in huge bacteriophages, which were shown to harbor genes encoding components of the translational machinery (Al-Shayeb et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Some phage S21 homologs contain KLY-like motifs.
claims.source: Inspection of sequence alignments reveals that some phage S21 homologs also contain KLY-like motifs (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The presence of phage S21 homologs containing KLY-like motifs is consistent with the host range of these phages.
claims.source: The presence of phage S21 homologs containing KLY-like motifs is consistent with the host range of these phages (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis and sequence data.

claims.claim: Ribosomal protein uS11 is a central component of the 30S subunit platform domain.
claims.source: Ribosomal protein uS11 is a central component of the 30S subunit platform domain and assembles cooperatively with ribosomal proteins uS6 and uS18 (Stern et al., 1988), preceding the binding of bS21 late in 30S subunit maturation (Held et al., 1973; Sashital et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Protein uS11 assembles cooperatively with ribosomal proteins uS6 and uS18.
claims.source: Ribosomal protein uS11 is a central component of the 30S subunit platform domain and assembles cooperatively with ribosomal proteins uS6 and uS18 (Stern et al., 1988), preceding the binding of bS21 late in 30S subunit maturation (Held et al., 1973; Sashital et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Protein uS11 makes intimate contact with 16S rRNA residues in a 3-helix junction that forms part of the 30S subunit E site.
claims.source: Protein uS11 makes intimate contact with 16S rRNA residues in a 3-helix junction that forms part of the 30S subunit E site and stabilizes the 16S rRNA that forms the platform component of the P site (Stern et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: An inspection of the 30S subunit map uncovered a previously unmodeled isoaspartyl residue in protein uS11, at the encoded residue N119.
claims.source: Remarkably, an inspection of the 30S subunit map uncovered a previously unmodeled isoaspartyl residue in protein uS11, at the encoded residue N119 (Figure 4; see Materials and methods), marking the first identified protein backbone modification in the ribosome.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 4 and by the modeling described in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: The isoaspartyl residue at position 119 in uS11 marks the first identified protein backbone modification in the ribosome.
claims.source: Remarkably, an inspection of the 30S subunit map uncovered a previously unmodeled isoaspartyl residue in protein uS11, at the encoded residue N119 (Figure 4; see Materials and methods), marking the first identified protein backbone modification in the ribosome.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, based on the structural data.

claims.claim: It has been known that the isoaspartate modification can exist in uS11.
claims.source: While it has been known that this modification can exist in uS11 (David et al., 1999), its functional significance has remained unclear, and prior structures did not have the resolution to pinpoint its exact location.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Prior structures did not have the resolution to pinpoint the exact location of the isoaspartate in uS11.
claims.source: While it has been known that this modification can exist in uS11 (David et al., 1999), its functional significance has remained unclear, and prior structures did not have the resolution to pinpoint its exact location.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about prior work.

claims.claim: Conversion of asparagine to isoaspartate inserts an additional methylene group into the backbone (the Cβ position) and generates a methylcarboxylate side chain.
claims.source: Conversion of asparagine to isoaspartate inserts an additional methylene group into the backbone (the Cβ position) and generates a methylcarboxylate side chain (Reissner and Aswad, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemistry of isoaspartate formation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In the present map, the shapes of the backbone density and proximal residues in the chain reveal the presence of the additional methylene in the isoaspartate.
claims.source: In the present map, the shapes of the backbone density and proximal residues in the chain reveal the presence of the additional methylene, allowing it the flexibility to pack closely with the contacting rRNA nucleotides (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: A 30S-focused reconstruction using only early movie frames shows improved density for the isoaspartate sidechain, albeit at slightly lower resolution overall.
claims.source: A 30S-focused reconstruction using only early movie frames, in which damage to carboxylates would not be as severe (Marques et al., 2019), shows improved density for the IAS sidechain, albeit at slightly lower resolution overall (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and by the rationale that early frames have less radiation damage.

claims.claim: Investigation of residues flanking the isoaspartate in uS11 reveals near-universal conservation in bacteria, chloroplasts, and mitochondria.
claims.source: Investigation of residues flanking the isoaspartate in uS11 reveals near-universal conservation in bacteria, chloroplasts, and mitochondria (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the isoaspartate may contribute to 30S subunit assembly or stability.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence logos and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The isoaspartate in uS11 may contribute to 30S subunit assembly or stability.
claims.source: Investigation of residues flanking the isoaspartate in uS11 reveals near-universal conservation in bacteria, chloroplasts, and mitochondria (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the isoaspartate may contribute to 30S subunit assembly or stability.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the conservation pattern and structural context.

claims.claim: The isoaspartate allows high shape complementarity including van der Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds between this region of uS11 and the 16S rRNA it contacts.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, the isoaspartate allows high shape complementarity including van der Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds between this region of uS11 and the 16S rRNA it contacts, which involves three consecutive purine-purine base pairs in bacteria (Supplementary file 2), and a change in rRNA helical direction that is capped by stacking of histidine 118 in uS11 on a conserved purine (A718 in E. coli; Figure 4B, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 4B and the sequence analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: The sequence motif in bacterial uS11 containing the isoaspartate is also conserved in a domain-specific manner in archaea and eukaryotes.
claims.source: Strikingly, the sequence motif in bacterial uS11 is also conserved in a domain-specific manner in archaea and eukaryotes (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as are the rRNA residues near the predicted isoAsp (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence logos shown in Figure 4C and the phylogenetic analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The rRNA residues near the predicted isoaspartate are conserved in archaea and eukaryotes.
claims.source: Strikingly, the sequence motif in bacterial uS11 is also conserved in a domain-specific manner in archaea and eukaryotes (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as are the rRNA residues near the predicted isoAsp (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: Remodeling the isoaspartate motifs in maps from recently-published cryo-EM reconstructions of an archaeal 30S ribosomal subunit complex and a yeast 80S ribosome complex shows that the isoaspartate also seems to be present in these organisms based on the residue-level correlation between map and model.
claims.source: Remodeling the isoAsp motifs in maps from recently-published cryo-EM reconstructions of an archaeal 30S ribosomal subunit complex at 2.8 Å resolution (Nürenberg-Goloub et al., 2020) and a yeast 80S ribosome complex at 2.6 Å resolution (Tesina et al., 2020) shows that the isoaspartate also seems to be present in these organisms based on the residue-level correlation between map and model (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the remodeling analysis and correlation plots shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic data and structural data indicate that the isoaspartate in uS11 is nearly universally conserved.
claims.source: Taken together, the phylogenetic data and structural data indicate that the isoaspartate in uS11 is nearly universally conserved, highlighting its likely important role in ribosome assembly and function.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined phylogenetic and structural evidence.

claims.claim: The E. coli 30S ribosomal subunit has eleven post-transcriptionally modified nucleotides in 16S rRNA.
claims.source: The E. coli 30S ribosomal subunit has eleven post-transcriptionally modified nucleotides in 16S rRNA, all of which can be seen in the present maps or inferred from hydrogen bonding patterns in the cases of many pseudouridines.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data and is consistent with known modifications.

claims.claim: Two methylated nucleotides–m7G527 and m62A1519–appear not to be fully modified, based on the density at ~2.1 Å resolution.
claims.source: Interestingly, two methylated nucleotides–m7G527 and m62A1519–appear not to be fully modified, based on the density at ~2.1 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: In the map, m7G527 appears partially methylated.
claims.source: In the map, m7G527 appears partially methylated, and m62A1519 lacks one of the two methyl groups.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density.

claims.claim: m62A1519 lacks one of the two methyl groups.
claims.source: In the map, m7G527 appears partially methylated, and m62A1519 lacks one of the two methyl groups.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density.

claims.claim: Loss of methylation at m7G527 has been shown to confer low-level streptomycin resistance.
claims.source: Loss of methylation at m7G527, which is located near the mRNA decoding site, has been shown to confer low-level streptomycin resistance (Okamoto et al., 2007), and possibly neomycin resistance in some cases (Mikheil et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Loss of methylation at m7G527 possibly confers neomycin resistance in some cases.

claims.claim: The map-to-model FSC metric has been described for some time but is not routinely used in the ribosome field.
claims.source: With regard to resolution, in this work, we have supplemented the reporting of the 'gold-standard' FSC with map-to-model FSC curves for our maps and for comparisons to previous work. Although the map-to-model FSC metric has been described for some time, it is not routinely used in the ribosome field (Halfon et al., 2019; Loveland et al., 2020; Nürenberg-Goloub et al., 2020; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020; Tesina et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the current practices in the field, supported by citations.

claims.source: For example, maps from recent cryo-EM reconstructions of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit report resolutions of ~2.1 Å–2.3 Å but the deposited models reach global resolutions of ~2.3 Å–2.5 Å by the map-to-model FSC criterion (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020; see Materials and methods; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the map-to-model FSC calculations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: For the 2.1 Å map of the E. coli 50S subunit based on half-map FSC values, the map-to-model FSC fit of the present 50S subunit model to that map has a higher resolution (2.07 Å), compared to the deposited model (2.29 Å).
claims.source: Notably, for the 2.1 Å map of the E. coli 50S subunit based on half-map FSC values (Pichkur et al., 2020), the map-to-model FSC fit of our 50S subunit model to that map has a higher resolution (2.07 Å), compared to the deposited model (2.29 Å, PDB entry 6xz7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the map-to-model FSC calculations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Model refinement procedures leverage well-defined chemical properties that are entirely independent of the map and should ensure realism.
claims.source: Additionally, while the map-to-model FSC calculations carry intrinsic bias from the model's dependence on the map, model refinement procedures leverage well-defined chemical properties (i.e. bond lengths, angles, dihedrals, and steric restraints) that are entirely independent of the map and should ensure realism.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for using the map-to-model FSC.

claims.claim: Methods for refining heterogeneous maps have proliferated, but ways to work with and create a model from many maps of the same complex have not yet been standardized and require substantial manual intervention.
claims.source: Aside from global high resolution, the conformational heterogeneity of the ribosome also calls attention to the tools used for working with complexes that display variable resolution. Methods for refining heterogeneous maps have proliferated, including multi-body refinement (Nakane et al., 2018) and 3D variability analysis (Punjani and Fleet, 2020) among others, but ways to work with and create a model from many maps of the same complex have not yet been standardized and require substantial manual intervention.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the current state of methods in the field.

results.result: The E. coli 70S ribosome structure was determined by cryo-EM to a global resolution of 2.0 Å (1.98 Å by GS-FSC, 2.04 Å by map-to-model FSC), with local resolution reaching 1.8 Å in the best-resolved regions of the 50S subunit core.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent resolution metrics (GS-FSC and map-to-model FSC) consistently support the claimed resolution. The FSC curves, local resolution maps, and visual features in the density (holes in aromatic rings, clear ribose puckers) all corroborate the high resolution achieved.

results.result: The high-resolution cryo-EM maps reveal unambiguous positioning of protein and RNA residues, detailed chemical interactions, and post-transcriptional/post-translational modifications.
results.evaluation: The claim is supported by visual features characteristic of high-resolution structures (holes in aromatic rings, ribose puckers, directional phosphate oxygens) and detailed figures showing clear density for individual residues and modifications throughout the manuscript.

results.result: An isoaspartyl residue at position 119 in ribosomal protein uS11 represents the first identified protein backbone modification in the ribosome and is nearly universally conserved across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: The isoaspartate is clearly visible in the cryo-EM density showing the additional methylene group in the backbone (C62). Phylogenetic analysis demonstrates near-universal conservation of the sequence motif across all domains of life (C64, C67, C68). Remodeling into archaeal and eukaryotic ribosome maps shows improved fit with the isoaspartate (C69, C146), providing strong convergent evidence for universal conservation.

results.result: A thioamide backbone substitution between Met82 and Gly83 in ribosomal protein uL16 represents the first example of this modification in a ribosomal protein, supported by both cryo-EM density and mass spectrometry data.
results.evaluation: The thioamide is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence: (1) cryo-EM density consistent with a thiocarbonyl sulfur atom, (2) mass spectrometry showing a +16 Da mass shift consistent with O→S conversion rather than oxidation, and (3) fragmentation spectra localizing the modification to the Met82-Gly83 bond. The convergence of structural and analytical evidence strongly supports this novel finding.

results.result: The isopeptide modification in uS11 is likely conserved in all domains of life and may contribute to 30S subunit assembly or stability.
results.evaluation: While phylogenetic conservation is well-demonstrated (C64, C67-C70), the functional role remains speculative. The claim that it 'may contribute to assembly or stability' (C65) is based on conservation patterns and structural context but lacks direct experimental validation. The functional significance requires future experimental work.

results.result: The complete C-terminal structure of protein bS21 was resolved, revealing a conserved RLY (or KLY in Betaproteobacteria) motif that makes specific contacts with 16S rRNA helix h37 and nucleotide A1167, with similar motifs found in phage S21 homologs consistent with their host range.
results.evaluation: The structural data clearly shows the C-terminal helix and RLY motif contacts with rRNA (C43-C47, Figure 3). Sequence alignments demonstrate phylum-specific conservation of RLY in Gammaproteobacteria and KLY in Betaproteobacteria (C48-C49), and the presence of KLY-like motifs in phage homologs correlates with their predicted host range (C52-C53), providing coherent structural and phylogenetic support.

results.result: Two methylated nucleotides in 16S rRNA (m7G527 and m62A1519) appear hypomodified, with m7G527 partially methylated and m62A1519 lacking one of two methyl groups.
results.evaluation: The hypomodification is directly observed in the cryo-EM density at ~2.1 Å resolution (C72, Figure 1—figure supplement 5). The observation that m62A1519 is singly methylated while m62A1518 is fully methylated (C86) is clearly visible in the maps and represents a novel finding about the in vivo methylation status of assembled ribosomes.

results.result: The β-methylthio-Asp modification at position 89 in uS12 appears hypomodified based on weak density for the β-methylthio group.
results.evaluation: The observation is directly supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6, where the β-methylthio group has weaker density compared to adjacent fully modified residues.

results.result: P-site tRNA binding involves extensive direct contacts between the tRNA anticodon stem-loop and both 30S subunit head and platform domains, with specific interactions mediated by uS9 residues Lys129 and Arg130.
results.evaluation: The structural data in Figure 2 clearly shows the extensive contacts and specific interactions, including Arg130 stacking with U33 and forming hydrogen bonds with the P-site ASL. The absence of density for uS13 and uS19 C-terminal tails (C37) is consistent with their lack of specific contacts in the unrotated state.

results.result: A-site tRNA interactions with the 30S subunit are highly localized to specific rRNA helices (h44, h18, H69), with contacts to the head domain being entirely solvent-mediated except for nucleotide C1054.
results.evaluation: The structural model shows the localized direct interactions at the decoding center and the extensive solvent-mediated contacts with the head domain (Figure 2E). This is consistent with known weaker A-site binding and the need for conformational dynamics during decoding.

results.result: High-resolution modeling of paromomycin reveals the complete structure including ring IV and surrounding solvation, with ring IV adopting a chair conformation and the N6''' group forming contacts with G1489-U1490 phosphate groups.
results.evaluation: The focused-refined 30S subunit map allows unambiguous modeling of the entire paromomycin molecule including ring IV for the first time (C98, Figure 5C-D). The specific contacts of the N6''' group with phosphate backbones are clearly shown in the structural model (C100, Figure 5D), though ring IV remains the least ordered of the four rings (C97).

results.result: The maps reveal extensive solvation of the 30S ribosomal subunit, with thousands of water molecules, dozens of magnesium ions, and polyamines modeled.
results.evaluation: The extensive solvation is documented in the models and figures (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2) with specific numbers provided in Table 3. This represents a significant advance over prior structures where 30S solvation was not extensively modeled.

results.result: The maps reveal detailed interactions between the ribosomal subunits, including contacts with A-site and P-site tRNAs, mRNA, and dynamic intersubunit bridges (H69, H34, A-site finger).
results.evaluation: The structural models show detailed interactions at the subunit interface, with H69 and H34 bridge better defined in the 30S-focused maps (C108, C110), indicating their conformational alignment with the small subunit. Specific contacts like C888 of the A-site finger with uS13 are clearly resolved (C113, Figure 6B).

results.result: The 50S subunit core reaches 1.8 Å resolution, revealing unprecedented structural details superior to prior X-ray crystallography, including conserved water molecules and ions in the peptidyl transferase center.
results.evaluation: The local resolution maps and comparison with prior structures support the superior quality of the present maps (C116). The identification of conserved solvent positions across phylogenetically diverse ribosomes (C118, Figure 7) demonstrates the level of detail achieved and its utility for comparative analysis.

results.result: Some regions of the RNA backbone show weak or broken density despite high overall resolution, which persists in low-dose reconstructions, suggesting this reflects RNA conformational flexibility rather than radiation damage.
results.evaluation: The observation is documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 7, and the persistence of similar patterns in reconstructions from the first 2-3 frames (low dose) supports the interpretation that this reflects structural disorder rather than beam damage (C124, C159). The correlation with regions lacking close contacts to other parts of the structure (C160) further supports this interpretation.

results.result: E. coli protein YcaO is a candidate enzyme for catalyzing uL16 thioamidation, with YcaO genes in Gammaproteobacteria colocalizing with the focA-pfl operon, suggesting the modification may be conserved only in Gammaproteobacteria.
results.evaluation: While YcaO is a reasonable candidate based on its known thioamidation activity (C133), the evidence is circumstantial. The phylogenetic separation and operon structure (C136-C138) suggest limited conservation, but direct experimental validation of YcaO's role in uL16 modification is lacking. This remains a hypothesis requiring future testing.

results.result: The final maps were generated by merging two separately prepared 70S ribosome complexes with different P-site tRNA substrates, both yielding structures in the same functional state, with focused refinement substantially improving 30S subunit map quality.
results.evaluation: The experimental design is clearly described and the merging of datasets is justified by the lack of resolved tRNA 3'-CCA ends in individual maps (C21). The improvement from focused refinement is documented in the resolution analysis (C25, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

results.result: Hypomodifications of m7G527, m62A1519, and β-methylthio-Asp89 could confer antibiotic resistance to streptomycin and kasugamycin without severely affecting ribosome assembly or function.
results.evaluation: While the hypomodifications are clearly observed (C72-C74, C78), the proposed resistance mechanisms are speculative (C80, C89, C149). The claims are based on prior knowledge of resistance mechanisms and structural context but lack direct experimental validation in the present study. These are hypotheses for future testing rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: The observed interactions between paromomycin N6''' amino group and the phosphate backbone of G1489-U1490 are likely responsible for known susceptibility to N6''' modification.
results.evaluation: The structural observation of specific contacts (C100, Figure 5D) combined with prior knowledge of aminoglycoside resistance mechanisms provides a reasonable mechanistic explanation for the known susceptibility to N6''' modification. This represents a structure-function correlation supported by the high-resolution data.

results.result: The location and conservation of bS21 near the ribosome binding site suggests potential roles in translation initiation and modulating 30S head domain dynamics, with phage S21 homologs possibly contributing to specialized translation or phage defense evasion.
results.evaluation: While the structural and phylogenetic data are solid (C43-C53), the proposed functional roles are speculative (C152, C153, C155, C156). The structural location suggests possible functions, but these remain hypotheses requiring experimental validation. The statement that these findings 'raise new questions' is more accurate than claiming demonstrated functions.

results.result: Map-to-model FSC analysis shows that recent bacterial ribosome structures have deposited models with lower resolution (2.3-2.5 Å) than their reported map resolutions (2.1-2.3 Å), with the present 50S model fitting a prior 2.1 Å map better (2.07 Å) than the deposited model (2.29 Å).
results.evaluation: The map-to-model FSC calculations are clearly documented (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and demonstrate that the present model achieves better correlation with a prior published map than the originally deposited model (C163). This supports the utility of map-to-model FSC as a complementary metric to half-map FSC for assessing model quality.

results.result: It is unclear whether the isoAsp modification in uS11 occurs spontaneously or requires enzymatic catalysis.
results.evaluation: This accurately reflects the current state of knowledge. While the modification is clearly present and conserved, the mechanism of formation remains unknown. The slow spontaneous rate (C142-C143) raises questions about whether an enzyme accelerates the process, but no such enzyme has been identified.

results.result: The high resolution achieved has potential for informing structure-activity relationships in antibiotic research, advancing aminoglycoside development, and aiding development of de novo RNA modeling tools.
results.evaluation: These are reasonable assessments of the potential applications of the work. The level of detail achieved (e.g., complete paromomycin structure with solvation, hypomodifications affecting antibiotic resistance) does provide a foundation for future drug development and methods development, though these remain prospective applications rather than demonstrated outcomes.
